bib.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

question: How does Transformer language-model cross-entropy loss depend on model size, dataset size, training compute and architecture, and how should a fixed compute budget be allocated?
hypothesis: Loss follows smooth power laws in N, D and C that are largely independent of architectural shape, so that compute-optimal training favours very large models trained on modest data and stopped short of convergence.
contributions: Performance depends strongly on scale (N, D, C) and weakly on model shape
Smooth power laws in N, D, C over many orders of magnitude
Universality of overfitting: penalty depends on N^0.74/D
Universality of training: learning curves are power laws with parameters roughly independent of model size
Transfer to other distributions improves with in-distribution loss at a constant offset
Large models are more sample efficient; compute-efficient training stops far short of convergence
Optimal batch size is a power of the loss only, about 1-2 million tokens at convergence for the largest models

method.summary: Train many decoder-only Transformers (and some LSTMs and Universal Transformers) on WebText2 with varied size, shape, data subset size, context and batch size; fit power laws to test loss, and derive compute-optimal allocation using the critical batch size of McCandlish et al. 2018.
method.task: autoregressive next-token language modelling (cross-entropy in nats)

datasets.name: WebText2
datasets.split: 6.6e8 tokens reserved as test set; dataset-size experiments use fixed subsets from 22 million to 23 billion tokens
datasets.source: Reddit outbound links with at least 3 karma, through Oct 2018; text extracted with Newspaper3k
datasets.preprocessing: reversible tokenizer of Radford et al. 2019, BPE, vocab 50257

datasets.name: Books Corpus, Common Crawl, English Wikipedia, Internet Books
datasets.split: similarly prepared samples; models trained only on WebText2
datasets.source: Zhu et al. 2015; Common Crawl Foundation; public Internet books

models.name: decoder-only Transformer
models.architecture: decoder-only Transformer, N ~ 12 n_layer d_model^2 with d_attn = d_ff/4 = d_model
models.layers: shapes from (n_layer, d_model) = (2, 128) up to (6, 4288) through (207, 768); (48, 1600) is the GPT-2 shape
models.context: 1024 tokens (n_ctx) for most runs; n_ctx = 8 for some

models.name: LSTM
models.architecture: LSTM, 1/2/4 layers, same data and context

training.objective: autoregressive log-likelihood (cross-entropy) averaged over a 1024-token context
training.optimizer: Adam; Adafactor for largest models (more than 1B parameters) because of memory
training.lr: rule of thumb LR(N) ~ 0.003239 - 0.0001395 log(N) for most runs (Eq D.1); breaks down for N > 1e10
training.lr_schedule: 3000 step linear warmup then cosine decay to zero
training.batch_size: 512 sequences of 1024 tokens (2^19 tokens) for most runs; varied to measure critical batch size
training.tokens: inferred: 2.5e5 steps x 2^19 tokens = about 1.3e11 tokens per standard run
training.dropout: 10% dropout in the L(N, D) overfitting experiments
training.regularisation: early stopping when test loss stops decreasing (dataset-size experiments); regularisation not otherwise tuned
training.compute: C ~ 6NBS non-embedding FLOPs, quoted in PF-days (1 PF-day = 8.64e19 FLOPs); runs span about eight orders of magnitude in Cmin
training.seeds: run-to-run loss variation roughly 0.02 (Sec 4.2) or 0.05 (Fig 22 caption); multiple runs averaged for smaller differences

other.excluded from fits: 1-layer models; largest models not trained to convergence

metrics.name: test cross-entropy loss
metrics.definition: nats per token averaged over a 1024-token context on WebText2 test (6.6e8 tokens) and other text distributions

eval.protocol: Fit power laws to early-stopped or converged test loss over a grid of N, D, S; compare fits against logarithmic alternatives; no significance tests.

evidence.quote: a batch size of 512 sequences of 1024 tokens
We regularize all our models with 10% dropout

results.claim: Loss as a power law in non-embedding parameters N (trained to convergence on a large dataset).
results.setup: WebText2, 1024-token context, models up to 1.5B non-embedding parameters trained to near convergence; Nc ~ 8.8e13 (tokenization-dependent)
results.note: Table 2 joint fit to L(N, D) gives alpha_N = 0.076, Table 3 L(N, S) gives 0.077.

results.claim: Loss as a power law in dataset size D with early stopping.
results.setup: 36-layer, 1280-wide model on fixed WebText2 subsets, stopped when test loss ceased to decrease; Dc ~ 5.4e13 tokens
results.note: The joint L(N, D) fit (Table 2) gives alpha_D = 0.103.

results.claim: Loss as a power law in optimally allocated compute Cmin.
results.setup: large dataset, optimally sized model, batch size far below critical; Cmin_c ~ 3.1e8 PF-days
results.note: Theory from L(N, Smin) predicts 0.054 (Eq 6.4) and 0.052 (Eq B.7); fixed-batch compute fit gives alpha_C = 0.057 (Table 5).

results.claim: Doubling parameters shrinks loss by a factor of about 0.95.
results.setup: from alpha_N = 0.076 under the L(N) law
results.quote:
doubling the number of parameters yields a loss that
is smaller by a factor 2−αN = 0.95

results.claim: Compute-optimal model size grows as Cmin^0.73.
results.setup: fit to Fig 14, batch-adjusted Cmin (training at critical batch size); N_opt = 1.3e9 * Cmin^0.73 params with Cmin in PF-days. Fixed-batch C gives 0.88.

results.claim: Each 10x of compute should give about 5x model size and only about 2x data examples.
results.setup: compute-efficient frontier, Fig 14
results.quote: increasing by 5x for each 10x increase in compute

results.claim: Batch size and serial steps for compute-efficient training grow as Cmin^0.24 and Cmin^0.03.
results.setup: empirically optimal values; the measured step exponent may be consistent with zero
results.quote:
N ∝C0.73
min , B ∝C0.24
min , and S ∝C0.03
results.note: quote spans a line break in the text; see also Eq 6.2.

results.claim: Data needed to avoid overfitting grows sublinearly in model size; D >~ 5e3 N^0.74.
results.setup: to stay within 0.02 of converged loss (seed variation), 10% dropout, early stopping, WebText2

results.claim: Increasing model size 8x needs only about 5x more data to avoid overfitting penalty.
results.setup: penalty depends on N^0.74/D
results.quote:
every time we increase the
model size 8x, we only need to increase the data by roughly 5x to avoid a penalty

results.claim: Joint fit to L(N, D) parameters.
results.setup: early-stopped, 10% dropout; poor fit for datasets reduced by 1024x (about 2e7 tokens, 40 updates per epoch)

results.claim: L(N, S) fit parameters for learning curves in the infinite data limit.
results.setup: stable Adam-trained runs, all steps after warmup, Smin adjusted to large batch

results.claim: Critical batch size is a power law in the loss and about doubles for every 13% decrease in loss.
results.setup: measured on 3M and 85M parameter models; independent of model size except through loss
results.note: Appendix prints B* = 2.1e8 tokens; Fig 10 caption: doubling per 13% loss decrease.

results.claim: Compute-efficient training stops about 10% above the converged loss.
results.setup: derived from the L(N, S) fit (Appendix B.2)
results.quote:
we should train to a ﬁxed percentage αN
αS ≈10% above
the converged loss

results.claim: Compared with training to 2% of convergence, compute-efficient training uses 7.7x fewer updates, 2.7x more parameters and 65% less compute for the same loss.
results.setup: model prediction using f = 10% vs f' = 2%
results.quote:
7.7x fewer parameter updates, 2.7x more parameters, and 65% less
compute to reach the same loss

results.claim: Models 0.6x to 2.2x the optimal size can be trained with only 20% more compute.
results.setup: from Eq B.16
results.quote:
Models between 0.6x and 2.2x the optimal size can be used with only a
20% increase in compute budget
results.note: A 2.2x larger model needs 45% fewer steps at 20% more compute.

results.claim: Loss depends only weakly on model shape: aspect ratio can vary by 40x while loss changes only a few percent.
results.setup: fixed N (25M and 50M parameter models); (6, 4288) vs the (48, 1600) model of GPT-2
results.quote:
an (nlayer, dmodel) = (6, 4288) reaches a
loss within 3% of the (48, 1600) model
results.note: Fig 5 text: 22% additional compute compensates for 1% loss increase.

results.claim: Extrapolated scaling laws collide: compute-efficient L(Cmin) meets the data-limited L(D) at roughly 1e4 PF-days, 1e12 parameters, 1e12 tokens, 1.7 nats/token.
results.value: C* ~ 1e4 PF-days; N* ~ 1e12; D* ~ 1e12; L* ~ 1.7 nats/token
results.setup: extrapolation; authors say numbers vary by an order of magnitude in either direction
results.note: Conjecture only: authors suggest L* might estimate the entropy per token of natural language.

results.claim: Data use for single-epoch compute-efficient training grows as Cmin^0.26-0.27.
results.setup: training at critical batch size, never re-using data
results.note: Eq 6.7 prints 0.26; Table 6 prints pD = 0.27 and De = 2e10; Sec 1.1 says D ~ C^0.27. Quote here is Eq 6.6, the overfitting-safe requirement of Cmin^0.54.

results.claim: Learning rate rule: larger models need smaller LR.
results.setup: used for most runs; fails for N > 1e10

results.claim: Estimated seed-to-seed loss variation.
results.setup: Section 4.2 estimate; Fig 22 caption says run-to-run variation at the 0.05 level for a 3M model
results.quote: the loss with different random seeds is roughly 0.02
results.note: Two figures in the paper: 0.02 (Sec 4.2) and 0.05 (Fig 22).

results.claim: Tokenization stats of WebText2.
results.setup: words defined with wc
results.quote: the WebText2 dataset has 1.4 tokens per word and 4.3 characters per token

limits: No theoretical understanding of any of the scaling laws (App C).
Bcrit(L) not trusted far outside the explored loss range.
Small-data regime not studied; L(N, D) fits poor at the smallest D; regularization and data augmentation not tuned.
Compute estimate 6NBS omits n_ctx terms, so confounded when n_ctx >~ 12 d_model.
Some hyperparameters (initialization scale, momentum) may not have been tuned; LR not tuned for short runs.
Only loss measured, not downstream task performance; authors note smooth loss may hide qualitative capability changes.
Fits are specific to WebText2 and its tokenization; Nc, Dc, Cc have no fundamental meaning.
Appendix B.4 text refers to 'Figure X' and 'Figure Y' (unresolved cross-references).
Dated: later work (Hoffmann et al. 2022) found a different compute-optimal ratio; this paper does not use Chinchilla-style per-run schedules.

terms.definition: Bcrit(L) = Emin/Smin; batch size at which training makes a roughly optimal time/compute tradeoff
an estimate of the minimum amount of non-embedding compute to reach a given value of the loss, as if trained at a batch size much less than the critical batch size
an estimate of the minimal number of training steps needed to reach a given value of the loss
number of model parameters, excluding all vocabulary and positional embeddings
1015 x 24 x 3600 = 8.64 x 10^19 floating point operations

figures.caption: Language modeling performance improves smoothly as we increase the model size, datasetset size, and amount of compute used for training.
figures.why: Three straight power-law lines summarise the whole paper.

figures.caption: As more compute becomes available, we can choose how much to allocate towards training larger models, using larger batches, and training for more steps.
figures.why: Shows for a billion-fold compute increase: >1,000,000x model size, 100x batch size, <10x serial steps.
